Hi Francois, hi listfolk!

Thanks for trying out readdst! We still consider it experimental at the
moment but we're very happy to have folks try it out! :)

Looks like you found a bug! We don't parse all of the possible DISTANCE
commands at the moment and your project has 2 that we hadn't handled yet
("Assign Output" and "Assign Stats"). I've added some code to ignore
these (as we don't save these files with readdst like DISTANCE does).

I've pushed some changes to github, if you get the latest version from
there:

library(devtools)
install_github("DistanceDevelopment/readdst")

you should be able to run your analysis.

Please do let me know if you have further issues and thanks again for
trying it out.

cheers,
--dave

Shawn, there is no need to create segmented areas for point data.  Methods for DSM for point data are outlined in

Hedley, S.L., Buckland, S.T. and Borchers, D.L. 2004.  Spatial distance sampling models.  In Advanced Distance Sampling, pp48-70.  S.T. Buckland, D.R. Anderson, K.P. Burnham, J.L. Laake, D.L. Borchers and L. Thomas (eds).  Oxford University Press, Oxford.

And there is some discussion of modelling options in section 3 of

Buckland, S.T., Oedekoven, C.S. and Borchers, D.L. 2016.  Model-based distance sampling.  Journal of Agricultural, Biological and Environmental Statistics 21, 58-75.

Steve Buckland

From: distance...@googlegroups.com [mailto:distance...@googlegroups.com] On Behalf Of Shawn O'Neil
Sent: 22 March 2017 22:30
To: distance-sampling <distance...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: [distance-sampling] DSM for point count data

Hi all,

I'm wondering if I can develop a DSM for point count data. I know it is possible to estimate the detection function, and it would appear that one could manipulate the data in some way as to create segmented areas using the point counts. For example:  https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/distance-sampling/dsm$20point$20count%7Csort:relevance/distance-sampling/dG-YCu9EV6w/FU8KF7q_BwAJ. My only idea was to generate a grid around the observation points and create the necessary fields for the segment.data object. Would it be a bad idea to try this? Are there other options?

Thanks & best regards,
Shawn

Fitting covariates to detection functions is difficult.  There are a number of "tricks" involved in doing so. Before having Distance try to fit models, do some exploratory analysis to see if covariates are correlated (they may be so by coincidence). Ask yourself how much your estimates of abundance are influenced by covariates included.

Hi all,

Could someone confirm me that a model without any adjustment term (ie key function only) is indeed
comparable (with AIC as returned by the AIC.dsmodel​ function) to a model including an adjustment term?

If that is the case, then I wonder if the following behaviour ("..." are exactly the same across all calls) is
really to be expected :

ds(..., key = 'hn', adjustment = NULL, ...)  --> AIC = -57.4
ds(..., key = 'hn', adjustment = 'cos', order = NULL, ...)  --> AIC = -57.4
ds(..., key = 'hn', adjustment = 'cos', order = 2, ...)  --> AIC = 618.3
ds(..., key = 'hn', adjustment = 'cos', order = 3, ...)  --> AIC = 620.2
ds(..., key = 'hn', adjustment = 'cos', order = 4, ...)  --> AIC = 622.2
ds(..., key = 'hn', adjustment = 'cos', order = 5, ...)  --> AIC = 625.2
ds(..., key = 'hn', adjustment = 'cos', order = c(2:6), ...)  --> AIC = 627.2

According to the doc of ds() calling the function with order = 4 for example should be expanded to 2, 3, 4, 5 and the
corresponding models should be compared... So why does the AIC.dsmodel function seem to return the highest  AIC
among the different adjustment orders ?
Shouldn't the no-adjustment model be considered as well by default, even if an adjustment and an order is specified? Or am I missing
something entirely?

Thanks in advance for your input on this

Olivier

messages.body_plain:
Hi Olivier, hi listfolk,

The AIC function in the Distance package will only return the AIC of the
best model, selection is done during the fitting (i.e., when ds() is
called). Adjustment selection will only take place if the order=NULL in
the call to ds() and in that case the selection process will be printed
to the screen and the model with no adjustments will be fitted first and
term selection will continue from least to most complex model (in the
sense of number of parameters); comparisons between AIC from
no-adjustment and adjustment-term models are fine. Setting order to be a
given value (e.g., 4) will expand the order out to be the appropriate
adjustment series (e.g., 2,3,4).

In your specific case, try

ds(...,key ='hn',adjustment ='cos',order =NULL,...)

and observe the console output.

Trying with the example data/code in ?ds(), I see:

 > ds.model <- ds(tee.data,4, order=NULL)
Starting AIC adjustment term selection.
Fitting half-normal key function
Key only model: not constraining for monotonicity.
AIC= 311.138
Fitting half-normal key function with cosine(2) adjustments
AIC= 313.124

Half-normal key function selected.
No survey area information supplied, only estimating detection function.

Hope this helps!

best,
--dave

Shane

Thanks for clarifying your question.  Unless you are overwhelmed by animals, I doubt that you have sufficient data to produce day-specific density estimates.

Open questions include: if there were insufficient captures to estimate a day-specific detection function, would you pool captures to fit a common detection function (that induces a dependence between daily estimates).  Is the population closed for the duration of the study?  If trapping is causing population depletion in the web centre where trap density is highest, I postulate that over time you would see captures increasingly at the edge of the web as animals not previously on the web come in--that will cause headaches for trying to fit a detection function in the latter days.

Your description suggests you had just a single web; I don't think I have any good advice for how to proceed.

messages.body_plain:
Dear list-folks and DS team,

I'm currently trying to produce a small report on DSM and its use with point-transect sampling (as I promised several months ago to Eric and I think it could be quite useful for sharing), as I did this during the 2016 workshop in St Andrews with the help of CREEM crew.

I ran the analysis in last August and here is the summary of the dsm function:
>summary(mod2.alt.km <http://mod2.alt.km>)

Family: quasipoisson
Link function: log

Formula:
Dhat ~ s(X, Y)

Parametric coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)   2.2500     0.1519   14.82   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

Approximate significance of smooth terms:
       edf Ref.df     F p-value
s(X,Y)   2      2 1.909   0.154

R-sq.(adj) =  0.0148   Deviance explained = 4.65%
GCV = 15.117  Scale est. = 17.901    n = 100

When I was trying to redo the analysis (I'm creating a knitr PDF with RStudio), the results were quite different, so I decided to run the exact same model and here is the summary:
> summary(mod2.alt.km.new <http://mod2.alt.km.new>)

Family: quasipoisson
Link function: log

Formula:
Dhat ~ s(X, Y)

Parametric coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)   2.1750     0.1438   15.12   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

Approximate significance of smooth terms:
         edf Ref.df    F p-value
s(X,Y) 11.88  16.18 1.31   0.208

R-sq.(adj) =   0.21   Deviance explained = 29.3%
-REML = 191.99  Scale est. = 14.545    n = 100

It appears that the estimation method has changed (REML instead of CGV.Cp) and the deviance explained is now much bigger, despite the dataset doesn't change.
The parametric coefficient is lower now and the array of estimated degrees of freedom for the model terms was only 2 and it now close to 12 ...

Furthermore, the predicted values are now different.
Here is the range of the predicted values with the "old" dsm:
> mod2.alt.km.pred <- predict(mod2.alt.km <http://mod2.alt.km>,preddata,preddata$area2)
> range(mod2.alt.km.pred)
[1]  5.263684 19.122528
> summary(mod2.alt.km.pred)
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.
  5.264   7.716   9.589  10.130  11.920  19.120
Densities are now estimated between 5 and 20 ind/km2.

Here is the range of the predicted values with the "new" dsm with exactly the same data for prediction:
> mod2.alt.km.pred.new <http://mod2.alt.km.pred.new> <- predict(mod2.alt.km.new <http://mod2.alt.km.new>,preddata,preddata$area2)  #relationship between Dhat and covariates
> range(mod2.alt.km.pred.new <http://mod2.alt.km.pred.new>)
[1]  3.715586 52.015128
> summary(mod2.alt.km.pred.new <http://mod2.alt.km.pred.new>)
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.
  3.716   6.198   8.917  10.430  11.540  52.020

Well, the lower density is now 3.7, not so different, but the larger predicted value is higher than 50 ind/km2, so about 2.5 times higher and it seems less biologically relevant ...
Despite the mean predicted densities are not so different, it seems that it works quite differently for both tails of the distribution of predicted values.

It is quite a big issue because when mapping such results, it can be quite difficult to explain why the scale of density is so big for some points.

Do you have any idea of what happened between August 2016 and now? The dsm package has been updated maybe and some function may have change ...

Thanks a lot for any clue !

Guillaume

Second announcement:

New information contained in this notice:
  - We are preparing a new version of the Distance for Windows (Distance
7.1) for use in this workshop.  It will have additional features for
density surface modelling and distance sampling simulation.  Follow
progress of the new version via the Twitter feed @DistanceSamp
  - As preparation for this intermediate workshop, we hope to have
introductory workshop materials freely-available online before the end
of June.  Until those introductory materials are available, there are a
series (~7) of video lectures at this YouTube channel
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL8k5p7gTuzQyvDreXY4F_oHSQ6ycovBw8
  - For those unable to travel to St Andrews to attend the intermediate
workshop, a limited number of spaces are available to attend the
workshop via videoconference link.  Participants to the workshop via
this medium will have reduced one-on-one interaction with instructors.
Consequently, videoconference participants will receive a 25% discount
to their registration.  Recognise the videoconference will be conducted
in real time; if you are in time zones distant from Scotland, your sleep
patterns will need to adjust for that week.

----

The Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling
(CREEM) is hosting an intermediate-level workshop in the summer of 2017
in our purpose-built facilities at the University of St Andrews,
Scotland.  The workshops are taught by leading researchers in the field,
including Len Thomas (@len_thom) and Dave Miller (@millerdl), using
industry-standard software (visit http://distancesampling.org for more
details).

The five day workshop will start on Monday 31st July at 09:00, with
registration from 08:45, at CREEM, and finish on Friday 4th August at 17:00.

There are two pre-requisites for this workshop: a) understanding of
conventional distance sampling and b) basic competence with the R
programming language.  Pre-requisite (a) can be fulfilled by
understanding of fundamental materials presented in Buckland et al.
(2001, Chapters 1, 2, 4, 5 and 7) or Buckland et al. (2015, Chapters 1,
2, 4, 5 and 6) — e.g., through previous training or by independent study.

Pre-requisite (b) can be achieved by either working through
instructional materials in R available at https://www.datacamp.com , or
by attending a free half-day tutorial preceding the workshop (30 July
2017 1400-1700). (details available at the link below)

The first day of the workshop will review fundamental principles of
distance sampling, analyses involving conventional distance sampling and
survey design.  Subsequently, attention will turn to simulation of
distance sampling surveys for design purposes (DSsim package), and to
survey and analysis methods for dealing with imperfect detection on the
trackline (double-observer methods) (MRDS package). Slightly more than
two days will be devoted to spatial (density surface) modelling of
distance sampling data (dsm package).  A blend of the latest version
Distance 7 and the R computing language will be employed.  Throughout
the workshop, there will be unstructured time, with instructors working
with participants on their specific problems.

Further details and registration instructions can be found at

http://creem2.st-andrews.ac.uk/intermediate-level-distance-sampling-training-workshop-2017/

messages.body_plain:
I don't have a good answer for you Shane.  Removal estimators work best when a large fraction of the original population is removed.  If your sampling is removing a large fraction of the population, you'll struggle to have sufficient detections to fit detection functions from point transect sampling.

If animals are coming onto your webs after other animals have been removed, it becomes difficult to believe the closure assumption implicit in both methods that presume the population is closed...  Those are the threats to your inference; I don't know how to overcome those threats.

On 30/03/2017 16:33, Shane Hill wrote:

> Sorry, I should have been as specific as possible from the start, it may help understand my questions. I have 12 sites with two webs at each site across the island of Hawaii. I am measuring the response of rat and mongoose densities to the presence/density of an invasive frog. Each site is spread across an "invasion front", where one web is within an invaded area and the other is without. Webs are placed far enough apart to assume independence.
>
> I see the problem now with day-specific estimates, the number of daily captures is unlikely to be enough to make a good estimate for each day. If that is the case, the question is, should I use the depletion data to get an index of abundance at each site or, as you said, pool the trapping data for the whole week to fit a common detection function.
>
> Thanks for the help!
> Shane
>
> On Thursday, March 30, 2017 at 7:33:23 AM UTC-6, Eric Rexstad wrote:
> >
> > Shane
> >
> > Thanks for clarifying your question.  Unless you are overwhelmed by animals, I doubt that you have sufficient data to produce day-specific density estimates.
> >
> > Open questions include: if there were insufficient captures to estimate a day-specific detection function, would you pool captures to fit a common detection function (that induces a dependence between daily estimates).  Is the population closed for the duration of the study?  If trapping is causing population depletion in the web centre where trap density is highest, I postulate that over time you would see captures increasingly at the edge of the web as animals not previously on the web come in--that will cause headaches for trying to fit a detection function in the latter days.
> >

My first thought was to stratify the  data by trap day so that I would get a density estimate for each day which would, in theory, be diminishing each day, and then use those estimates in a removal model in R to get an overall abundance for each site. What I would like to know is if there is a way to do this all in distance to avoid the need of switching between programs.

Hi Guillaume, hi listfolk,

Your diagnosis is correct: the switch from GCV.Cp to REML as default
smoothness selection method is the reason for this change.

I've had this question a few times, so I thought it best to write it up
as a wiki page on the dsm github site here:

https://github.com/DistanceDevelopment/dsm/wiki/Why-is-the-default-smoothing-method-%22REML%22-rather-than-%22GCV.Cp%22%3F

Comments on how to make this better/more accessible are very welcome,
though please direct them to me rather than the list.

cheers,
--dave
